paper.title: Statin use and in-hospital mortality in adults admitted with severe influenza: a multinational registry analysis

paper_doc.title: Statin use and in-hospital mortality in adults admitted with severe influenza: a multinational registry analysis
paper_doc.authors: Adaeze Okafor, Per Lindqvist, Sunita Raman, Claire Moreau, for the Severe Influenza Outcomes Registry investigators
paper_doc.abstract: Background: Statins have anti-inflammatory and endothelial effects that might improve outcomes in severe influenza, but trial evidence is lacking and observational studies have been small and confined to single countries. Methods: We analysed adults admitted with laboratory-confirmed influenza and at least one sign of severe disease to 61 hospitals in a multinational registry over four influenza seasons. Patients taking a statin before admission were compared with non-users using Cox regression weighted by the inverse probability of treatment, with in-hospital death as the primary outcome. Findings: Of 9412 eligible patients, 2874 (30.5%) were taking a statin at admission. In-hospital mortality was 7.9% among statin users and 10.6% among non-users. After weighting, statin use was associated with lower in-hospital mortality (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.91). The association was robust in sensitivity analyses. Interpretation: Prior statin use was associated with modestly lower in-hospital mortality in adults admitted with severe influenza. Randomised trials are needed before statins can be recommended as a treatment.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Seasonal influenza causes several million hospital admissions worldwide each year, and a substantial share of adults admitted with severe disease die in hospital or are discharged with lasting loss of function. Antiviral treatment shortens illness when started early, but many patients present too late for antivirals to change the course of their disease, and the damage seen in fatal cases is driven as much by the host inflammatory response as by viral replication. Treatments that modify that response have therefore attracted interest.
Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase and lower cholesterol, but they also reduce the production of inflammatory cytokines, stabilise the vascular endothelium and limit the recruitment of neutrophils into the lung in animal models of viral pneumonia. These pleiotropic effects suggest that patients already taking a statin when they fall ill might be partly protected against the most severe consequences of infection, and that starting a statin early in severe illness might help.
The evidence in people is mixed. Several cohort studies of patients admitted with influenza or community-acquired pneumonia have reported lower mortality among statin users, while others have found no association once frailty and access to care were taken into account. Most of these studies were drawn from a single country or a single health system, used administrative codes rather than laboratory confirmation, and could not measure disease severity at admission. Healthy-user effects, in which patients who take preventive medicines are healthier in ways that are hard to measure, are a well-known source of bias in this field.
A large, multinational registry with laboratory-confirmed cases and structured severity data offers a better chance to estimate the association while accounting for these sources of bias. We used such a registry to estimate the association between statin use before admission and in-hospital mortality among adults admitted with severe influenza, and to see whether the association differed by region, age, sex and the presence of cardiovascular disease.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text:
Registry and setting. The Severe Influenza Outcomes Registry enrols adults admitted with laboratory-confirmed influenza to participating hospitals in four world regions. Research nurses at each site record demographic data, medicines taken before admission, physiological measurements in the first 24 hours, treatments and outcomes using a standard electronic case report form. Data are checked centrally for completeness and range errors, and queries are returned to sites. The registry was approved by the ethics committee of each participating hospital, and individual consent was waived or obtained according to local requirements.
Participants. We included adults aged 18 years or older admitted between the start of the first influenza season and the end of the fourth season covered by the registry, with influenza confirmed by a molecular test and at least one sign of severe disease at admission: oxygen saturation below 92% on room air, a respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute or more, systolic blood pressure below 90 mm Hg, or a need for intensive care within 24 hours. We excluded patients transferred from another hospital after more than 24 hours, patients receiving end-of-life care at admission, and patients with missing statin data.
Exposure. Statin use was defined as a statin recorded in the list of medicines taken regularly in the 30 days before admission and confirmed against the pharmacy record or the patient's own supply. Patients whose statin was stopped during the admission remained in the statin group. We did not study statins started in hospital.
Outcomes. The primary outcome was death from any cause before discharge from hospital. Secondary outcomes were admission to intensive care after the first 24 hours, need for invasive mechanical ventilation, and length of hospital stay among survivors.
Covariates. We selected covariates in advance on the basis of a causal diagram: age, sex, body mass index, smoking, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, chronic lung disease, cardiovascular disease, cancer, frailty score, vaccination status for the current season, antiviral treatment within 48 hours of admission, days from symptom onset to admission, and physiological severity score at admission.
Statistical analysis. We estimated propensity scores for statin use with logistic regression on the covariates listed above and used stabilised inverse probability of treatment weights, truncated at the 1st and 99th percentiles. Balance was judged adequate when every standardised mean difference was below 0.1 after weighting. We fitted weighted Cox proportional hazards models for in-hospital death, with discharge alive treated as a competing event in a sensitivity analysis. Robust standard errors accounted for clustering by hospital. Missing covariate data (under 4% for any variable) were handled by multiple imputation with 20 imputed datasets. Prespecified subgroup analyses were by region, age group, sex and cardiovascular disease, with tests for interaction. Analyses used R version 4.0.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Participants. Of 11 236 adults admitted with laboratory-confirmed influenza and signs of severe disease during the study period, 9412 met the inclusion criteria and were analysed; 2874 (30.5%) were taking a statin at admission and 6538 were not. Statin users were older, more often men, and more likely to have diabetes, cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease. Statin users were also more likely to have been vaccinated for the current season. After weighting, all covariates were balanced. Table 1 shows the patients by region of the admitting hospital.

table.caption: Table 1. Patients by region of the admitting hospital

sections.heading: Primary outcome
sections.text: In total, 227 statin users (7.9%) and 693 non-users (10.6%) died in hospital. The median time to death was 9 days in both groups. In the weighted analysis, statin use was associated with a lower hazard of in-hospital death (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.91). Treating discharge alive as a competing event gave a similar estimate. Statin use was associated with a lower risk of invasive mechanical ventilation but not with admission to intensive care after the first 24 hours, and length of stay among survivors was similar in the two groups (Table 2).

table.caption: Table 2. Primary and secondary outcomes, weighted analysis

sections.heading: Subgroup analyses
sections.text: The association between statin use and in-hospital death was seen in every region, though its size varied (Table 3). Oceania was the region with the largest benefit, with an HR of 0.52. There was no evidence that the association differed by age group, sex or the presence of cardiovascular disease (all interaction p values above 0.2).

table.caption: Table 3. In-hospital death by region, weighted analysis

sections.heading: Sensitivity analyses
sections.text: The estimate for the primary outcome was little changed when we restricted the analysis to patients with complete covariate data, when we used propensity-score matching instead of weighting, when we excluded patients who received antivirals more than 48 hours after admission, and when we excluded the first influenza season. Adding a frailty score measured by the research nurse rather than taken from the clinical record also left the estimate unchanged. As a negative control outcome, statin use was not associated with hospital-acquired urinary tract infection, which argues against a large healthy-user effect. An E-value analysis indicated that an unmeasured confounder would need to be associated with both statin use and death by a risk ratio of about 1.8 to explain away the association.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Weighted cumulative incidence of in-hospital death among statin users and non-users over the first 30 days after admission.

sections.heading: Covariate balance
sections.text: Before weighting, statin users differed from non-users on most measured characteristics; the largest differences were in age, cardiovascular disease and diabetes. After weighting, every standardised mean difference was below 0.1 (Table 4). The distribution of weights was narrow, with a maximum stabilised weight of 4.2 before truncation, and the effective sample size after weighting was 8 960. Balance was similar in each imputed dataset.

table.caption: Table 4. Selected baseline characteristics before and after weighting

sections.heading: Subgroups by patient characteristics
sections.text: Figure 2 shows the hazard ratios for in-hospital death by age group, sex and the presence of cardiovascular disease. Estimates were similar in patients younger and older than 65 years, in men and women, and in patients with and without cardiovascular disease, and the confidence intervals overlapped widely. We did not analyse subgroups defined by statin type or dose, because these were recorded inconsistently across sites. A post hoc analysis restricted to patients who had received the current season's vaccine gave an estimate close to the main result.

figure.caption: Figure 2. Hazard ratios (95% CI) for in-hospital death with statin use, by age group, sex and cardiovascular disease. The vertical line marks the pooled estimate.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text:
Principal findings. In this multinational registry of more than 9000 adults admitted with severe influenza, patients who were taking a statin when they were admitted had a lower risk of dying in hospital than similar patients who were not, after accounting for a wide range of measured confounders. The association was robust to several sensitivity analyses and was not explained by the negative control outcome we examined. Statin use was also associated with a lower need for mechanical ventilation, which fits a protective effect on the lung, but not with later admission to intensive care.
Comparison with other studies. Our estimate lies within the range reported by earlier cohort studies, which have found associations ranging from no effect to a halving of mortality. The larger estimates came mainly from studies that relied on administrative codes and could not adjust for severity at admission. Our use of laboratory confirmation, structured severity data and a frailty score is likely to have reduced, though not removed, the confounding that inflated some earlier results.
Possible mechanisms. Statins reduce the production of interleukin 6 and other cytokines, improve endothelial function and reduce the expression of adhesion molecules. In mouse models of influenza, statins reduce lung injury without reducing viral load. A protective effect on the host response rather than on the virus would be consistent with the lower need for ventilation we observed.
Strengths and limitations. The strengths of this study are its size, its multinational design, laboratory confirmation of every case, and a prespecified analysis plan. Its main limitation is that it is observational: statin users differ from non-users in ways that can be hard to measure, and residual confounding cannot be excluded. We studied only patients already taking a statin, so our results say nothing about starting a statin in hospital. Statin dose, type and adherence were not recorded reliably enough to analyse. Hospitals that join a registry may differ from others, and the results may not apply to settings with fewer resources.
Implications. A modest association of this kind is not enough to recommend statins as a treatment for influenza, but it supports a randomised trial of continuing or starting statins in adults admitted with severe disease, and it suggests that clinicians should not stop a statin a patient already takes when they are admitted with influenza.
Future research. A pragmatic trial embedded in a registry of this kind could randomise admitted statin users to continuation or interruption, and statin-naive patients to a short course or usual care, at modest cost. Such a trial should measure inflammatory markers at admission and on day three, so that any benefit can be linked to the proposed mechanism, and should record statin type, dose and adherence. Studies in settings with fewer resources, where the burden of severe influenza is greatest and statins are cheap, are a particular priority. Linkage of registry data to longer-term outcomes, such as readmission and death within a year, would show whether any benefit seen in hospital persists after discharge.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Among adults admitted with severe influenza, prior statin use was associated with modestly lower in-hospital mortality. Randomised trials are needed to establish whether this association reflects a causal effect.

sections.heading: Contributors and funding
sections.text: AO and PL conceived the study. SR managed the registry data. AO and CM did the analyses. All authors interpreted the results and revised the manuscript. The registry is funded by public research grants; the funders had no role in the design, analysis or reporting of the study. The authors declare no competing interests. Data are available from the registry steering committee on reasonable request.

documents.title: Department of Error
documents.text:
Department of Error

Okafor A, Lindqvist P, Raman S, Moreau C. Statin use and in-hospital mortality in adults admitted with severe influenza: a multinational registry analysis. J Fake Med 2021; 14: 233–45—In this Article, 526 patients treated at two hospitals in Asia were wrongly recorded in the registry as treated in Oceania. In table 1, the number of patients from Asia should read 3644 (38.7%), not 3118 (33.1%), and the number from Oceania should read 58 (0.6%), not 584 (6.2%). In table 3, the Asia estimate should read 0.85 (0.72 to 1.00), not 0.86 (0.72 to 1.02), and the Oceania estimate, HR 0.52 (0.38 to 0.71), has been removed because 58 patients are too few to estimate it. The sentence in the Results that described Oceania as the region with the largest benefit has been deleted. The total number of patients, the pooled hazard ratio, the other results and the conclusions are unchanged. This Article has been corrected as of June 8, 2021.

draft_doc.running_head: Draft manuscript · not for circulation · version 0.4
draft_doc.title: Statin therapy and in-hospital outcomes of severe influenza in Australian and New Zealand hospitals: protocol for a retrospective cohort study
draft_doc.authors: Eleanor Harrington, Tamati Ngata, Lydia Chua
draft_doc.abstract: Introduction: Statins have anti-inflammatory and endothelial effects that may protect patients with severe influenza, but there are no estimates of this association from Australian and New Zealand hospitals, where patterns of statin prescribing, vaccination and influenza seasonality differ from those in the northern hemisphere. Methods and analysis: We will conduct a retrospective cohort study of adults admitted with laboratory-confirmed influenza to eight hospitals in Australia and New Zealand over five influenza seasons. The exposure is statin use in the 30 days before admission; the primary outcome is in-hospital death. We will use inverse probability of treatment weighting and Cox regression. Ethics and dissemination: The study has been approved by the relevant human research ethics committees. Results will be published in a peer-reviewed journal and shared with participating hospitals.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Influenza places a heavy seasonal load on hospitals in Australia and New Zealand. In a typical season, tens of thousands of adults are admitted with influenza, and older adults and those with chronic heart, lung or kidney disease account for most deaths [1, 2]. Antiviral treatment is recommended for all patients admitted with influenza, but many present several days after symptom onset, when the benefit of antivirals is small [3]. Much of the harm in severe influenza comes from the host inflammatory response, including cytokine release, endothelial injury and leakage of fluid into the lung [4, 5], which has led to interest in treatments that modify that response.
Statins are among the most widely prescribed medicines in both countries, taken by roughly one in four adults over 60 [6]. Beyond lowering cholesterol, statins reduce the production of inflammatory cytokines, improve endothelial function and limit the recruitment of neutrophils into the lung in experimental models of viral pneumonia [7, 8]. These effects have prompted the hypothesis that patients already taking a statin when they become unwell may be partly protected from the most severe consequences of influenza.
Observational studies have tested this hypothesis with mixed results. Studies of community-acquired pneumonia in Europe and North America have reported lower mortality among statin users in some cohorts [9, 10] but not in others once frailty was accounted for [11]. A cohort from a national health system in northern Europe found an association with lower mortality after influenza admission that weakened after adjustment for vaccination and prior health care use [12]. The healthy-user effect, in which people who take preventive medicines differ from those who do not in ways that are hard to measure, is a persistent source of bias in this field [13], and studies relying on administrative codes rather than laboratory confirmation are vulnerable to misclassification of the outcome population [14, 15].
Two randomised trials of statins in acute respiratory illness have been reported. One trial in ventilated patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome found no effect on mortality [16], and a smaller trial in patients admitted with pneumonia was stopped early for slow recruitment [17]. Neither trial was restricted to influenza, and neither tested statins in patients already taking them before admission, which is the question most relevant to everyday practice: whether a statin a patient already takes should be continued, and whether statin users can be expected to do better.
Australian and New Zealand hospitals have not contributed a dedicated estimate to this literature. The region differs from the northern hemisphere in ways that could matter: the timing of influenza seasons, the strains that circulate, vaccination coverage in older adults, and the prescribing of high-intensity statins [18, 19]. Indigenous Australians and Māori and Pacific peoples carry a disproportionate share of severe influenza and of cardiovascular disease [20], so an estimate from these populations would be of direct value to local clinicians and policy makers. The aim of this study is to estimate the association between statin use before admission and in-hospital death among adults admitted with severe influenza to hospitals in Australia and New Zealand.

sections.heading: 2. Rationale and hypothesis
sections.text:
The strongest signal for our region comes from the multinational registry analysis of Okafor et al. [21], which found that statin users admitted to hospitals in Oceania had the largest reduction in in-hospital mortality of any region (HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.71). This regional result is the main basis for our hypothesis that statin use is associated with a substantial reduction in in-hospital death among adults admitted with severe influenza in Australia and New Zealand, larger than the modest associations reported from European cohorts. If the regional result is confirmed in a dedicated local cohort, it would support continuing statins in admitted patients and would strengthen the case for including Australian and New Zealand sites in any future randomised trial.
We also hypothesise that statin use is associated with a lower need for invasive mechanical ventilation, in keeping with a protective effect on lung injury, and that the association is present in older adults, in patients with and without cardiovascular disease, and in Indigenous and non-Indigenous patients.

sections.heading: 3. Methods
sections.text:
3.1 Design and setting. This is a retrospective cohort study using linked clinical, laboratory and pharmacy data from eight public hospitals, five in Australia and three in New Zealand, over five influenza seasons. The hospitals include three tertiary referral centres and five regional hospitals, chosen to reflect the mix of metropolitan and rural patients in both countries.
3.2 Participants. We will include adults aged 18 years or older admitted with influenza confirmed by a molecular test within 72 hours of admission and with at least one sign of severe disease: oxygen saturation below 92% on room air, a respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute or more, systolic blood pressure below 90 mm Hg, or admission to intensive care within 24 hours. We will exclude patients transferred from another hospital after more than 24 hours, patients receiving end-of-life care at admission, and repeat admissions within the same season.
3.3 Exposure. Statin use is defined as a statin dispensed in the 90 days before admission according to linked pharmacy records, and recorded on the medication chart at admission. We will record the statin type and dose and classify intensity according to national guidelines [22].
3.4 Outcomes. The primary outcome is death from any cause before discharge. Secondary outcomes are invasive mechanical ventilation, admission to intensive care after the first 24 hours, length of stay among survivors, and death within 90 days of admission from linked death registrations.
3.5 Sample size. We expect about 3200 eligible admissions over five seasons, of whom about 25% will be statin users, with an in-hospital mortality of about 9% among non-users. With these numbers the study will have more than 80% power at a two-sided alpha of 0.05 to detect a hazard ratio of 0.70 or lower.
3.6 Statistical analysis. Covariates were chosen in advance from a causal diagram and include age, sex, ethnicity, area-level deprivation, rurality, body mass index, smoking, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, chronic lung disease, cardiovascular disease, cancer, frailty, influenza vaccination in the current season, antiviral treatment within 48 hours, days from symptom onset to admission and a physiological severity score. We will estimate propensity scores by logistic regression and use stabilised inverse probability of treatment weights [23]. Weighted Cox models will estimate the hazard ratio for in-hospital death, with robust standard errors clustered by hospital and discharge alive as a competing event in a sensitivity analysis. Missing covariate data will be handled by multiple imputation [24]. Prespecified subgroups are age group, sex, Indigenous status, cardiovascular disease and statin intensity. As a negative control outcome we will examine hospital-acquired urinary tract infection.

sections.heading: 4. Ethics and dissemination
sections.text: The study has been approved by the human research ethics committees responsible for each participating hospital, with a waiver of individual consent for the use of routinely collected data. Indigenous governance groups in both countries have reviewed the protocol, and results for Indigenous patients will be reported in partnership with them. Results will be submitted to a peer-reviewed journal, presented at national meetings and summarised for participating hospitals and consumer groups.

sections.heading: 5. Limitations
sections.text: As an observational study, this cohort cannot exclude residual confounding, including healthy-user effects that are not captured by our covariates. Pharmacy dispensing does not guarantee that patients took their statin. The number of deaths in some subgroups will be small, and subgroup estimates will be reported with that caution. The hospitals were not chosen at random, although they cover a broad range of settings.

says the draft's Rationale and hypothesis section relies on the removed Oceania estimate
tells the researcher to remove or rewrite the claim and hypothesis built on the Oceania result
must_not_include: says the notice is about a different paper or that it cannot tell which paper the notice concerns
says the pooled hazard ratio or the paper's conclusion changed
gives a corrected Oceania hazard ratio

expected.why: RE-changes-explained.md §1, C3: the notice's title is only "Department of Error", naming neither the paper nor the error, so the model must use update-to and the notice body (which names the article) to tie it to this paper and to learn what changed: Oceania's patients fall from 584 to 58 and its "HR 0.52" estimate is removed, while the pooled result stands. A data correction that removes a subgroup result but leaves the conclusions is medium. The draft's Rationale rests its hypothesis on that Oceania estimate (key_evidence, affected); key_evidence x medium = medium.
